topic.title: Transformations of Functions
topic.summary: How shifts, dilations, and reflections change a function's graph, its points, its domain and range, and its asymptotes.

lesson.title: Transformations of Functions
lesson.summary: How shifts, dilations, and reflections change a function's graph, its points, its domain and range, and its asymptotes.
learningGoals: Describe how adding to the input or output shifts the graph of a function.
Describe dilations and reflections that come from multiplying the input or the output.
Predict how a transformation changes points, asymptotes, domain, and range.
lesson.bigIdea: Changing a function's rule in a small way moves or reshapes its graph in a predictable way. Changes to the input act on the horizontal direction, and changes to the output act on the vertical direction.
lesson.context: Every function family in this course is built from a few basic graphs by transformations. Knowing how a change in the rule moves each point lets you describe a new function from one you already understand.

sections.title: Adding to the input or to the output translates the graph.

blocks.text: A translation slides every point of a graph the same distance without changing its shape. Adding a constant to the output, as in g(x) = f(x) + d, moves the graph up by d units (down if d is negative). Adding to the input, as in g(x) = f(x − c), moves the graph right by c units (left if c is negative).
The horizontal direction feels backward at first. For g(x) = f(x − 3), the output g(5) equals f(2), so the point (2, f(2)) of f appears at x = 5. Each point of f moves 3 units to the right.

blocks.caption: Points of f(x) = x² and of g(x) = f(x − 3) + 2

sections.takeaway: A change inside the parentheses moves the graph sideways in the opposite direction. A change outside moves it up or down.

sections.title: Multiplying the output or input stretches, compresses, or reflects the graph.

blocks.text: A dilation stretches or compresses a graph. In g(x) = a·f(x), every output is multiplied by a, so the graph is stretched vertically if |a| > 1 and compressed if |a| < 1. If a is negative, the graph is also reflected across the x-axis. A reflection flips the graph over a line.

In h(x) = f(bx), every input is multiplied by b before f acts, so each point moves to x-coordinate (original x)/b. The graph is compressed horizontally by a factor of 1/|b| when |b| > 1 and stretched when |b| < 1. If b is negative, the graph is reflected across the y-axis.

blocks.caption: Points of f(x) = 4 − x², of −2·f(x), and of f(2x)

sections.takeaway: Outside multiplication changes y-values. Inside multiplication changes x-values by the reciprocal.

sections.title: Combined transformations are read one piece at a time.

blocks.text: Many transformations combine a dilation, a reflection, and a translation. For g(x) = a·f(b(x − h)) + k, the factor b and the shift h act on the inputs, and a and k act on the outputs. A reliable method is to track a few key points of f, such as zeros and extreme points, and move each one.

Let f(x) = x² − 1, which has zeros at x = −1 and x = 1, and let g(x) = 2f(x − 3). The zeros of g occur where x − 3 = −1 or x − 3 = 1, so at x = 2 and x = 4. The vertex of f at (0, −1) moves to (3, −2), because the shift sends 0 to 3 and the dilation doubles −1.

sections.takeaway: Move the key points one transformation at a time, inside changes first for x-values and outside changes first for y-values.

sections.title: Transformations move the asymptotes and change the domain and range.
sections.conceptTitle: Effects on domain, range, and asymptotes

blocks.text: A horizontal translation moves vertical asymptotes by the same amount, and a vertical translation moves horizontal asymptotes. The parent function f(x) = 1/x has the vertical asymptote x = 0 and the horizontal asymptote y = 0. For g(x) = 1/(x − 2) + 3, the asymptotes are x = 2 and y = 3. The domain of g is all real numbers except 2, and its range is all real numbers except 3.
Output changes also change the range. The function f(x) = x² has range [0, ∞). For h(x) = −2f(x) + 3, the values −2x² are at most 0, so h has range (−∞, 3].

sections.takeaway: Apply the same transformation to the asymptotes, the domain, and the range as you apply to the points.

vocabulary.definition: A transformation that slides every point of a graph the same distance in the same direction.
A transformation that stretches or compresses a graph by multiplying all of its x-coordinates or all of its y-coordinates by a constant.
A transformation that flips a graph across a line, such as the x-axis or the y-axis.

connections.title: Forms that expose a shift
connections.body: In Topic 1.11, different forms of an expression showed different features. A rule written in terms of (x − 3) shows the sideways shift directly, while the expanded form hides it.
connections.transferQuestion: Why can a factored or shifted form be easier to read than an expanded one when you want to describe a graph?
connections.feedback: It displays the transformations and the key points directly, so you do not need to expand and compare.

connections.title: Transformations inside models
connections.body: In Topic 1.13, you will choose a function family for a data set. Knowing how transformations adjust a family lets you fit it to a situation.
connections.transferQuestion: If a basic model starts at the wrong place on the axes, which transformation would you use to fix that?
connections.feedback: A translation. A shift of the input or output moves the starting point.
